articles.title: Bangkok at breaking point as floods turn streets into stagnant lakes
articles.description: With 40 dead and a disaster declared across all 50 city districts, experts warn extreme flooding will only worsen across south-east Asia Bangkok is used to absorbing the sudden afternoon downpours that inundate the city during the rainy season. Even streets in many central high-rise districts can briefly turn into rivers, with rats and cockroaches racing out of sewers and taking temporary refuge on trees and buildings as the subterranean world is flushed out. But every city has a breaking point, and this year rain fell so fast and so hard that whole neighbourhoods of the Thai capital have been transformed, not into rivers, but stagnant lakes. In parts of the city, roughly 300mm of rain – the equivalent of half a year of average rainfall in London – fell in about two days. Continue reading...

articles.title: Don’t Worry, Everyone! Trump Says He Can Walk Up Ramps and Stairs
articles.description: The bar for America’s highest elected office keeps sinking. The nation’s totally healthy, very fit, 80-year-old president gave himself a little pat on the back Thursday after he managed to climb on the rally stage at the Peterbilt Motors manufacturing facility in Denton, Texas. The celebration came amid a dig at the health of his predecessor, former President Joe Biden. “Don’t forget, when Biden left the stage he spoke very shortly, like two minutes, one minute, as quickly as possible,” Trump said . “Could never find the stairs.” “I don’t have that problem. You know, these things—you know how many stairs they have?” Trump continued. “Look, I can go ramp, and I can go stair, I can go another stair, another stair in the back, I have a stair here—he could never find a stair.” "I can go ramp, I can go stairs" -- Trump's audience in Texas gives him an extremely tepid round of applause as he brags about being able to go up stairs without falling pic.twitter.com/SvQFajZZGO — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) October 1, 2026 Trump is the second oldest man to ever serve as America’s commander in chief. The octogenarian has spent hours at Walter Reed Medical Center on multiple occasions since he returned to office, has fallen asleep during more than a dozen critical meetings , appeared lost and disoriented around foreign heads of state, frequently slurs his speech, and seems to almost chronically suffer from discolored and bruised skin. His behavior has also grown increasingly erratic, as he has thrown cheap and petty insults at members of the press, challenged longstanding U.S. alliances, and even taken jabs at the pope. But Trump has nonetheless insisted that he is perfectly fit to keep the country’s most important job. Since 2024, the self-styled “stable genius” has “aced” several cognitive exams, though his recollections of the tests’ contents have called into question whether he actually took them at all. The American public is apparently wising up to Trump’s age: A national Strength in Numbers/Verasight poll conducted in July found that public perceptions of Trump’s mental health were on par with Biden’s, with 46 percent of respondents rating Trump’s mental sharpness as “poor.”

articles.title: These underwater umbrellas can shade coral reefs to protect them from bleaching
articles.description: Our oceans are incredibly hot , and that heat stress is a major threat to coral reefs. To truly protect corals, we need to address climate change as a whole. But in the meantime, scientists say they can give reefs a bit of relief simply by providing them with some shade. Researchers recently tested this concept in the Florida Keys with underwater “umbrellas” made out of shade cloths—the same textiles used on farms or in home gardens to protect plants from the harsh sun. Those umbrellas floated above individual corals. Though heat stress during the summer of the study was the second highest on record, the corals under the shade lost less color than expected, and in some cases, even recovered some of their color. That’s significant, because the loss of color results from the death of algae that live with corals. Providing shade doesn’t actually cool the water, says Karen Neely, a research scientist with Nova Southeastern University in Florida and lead author of the study on this experiment, published today in the journal Frontiers in Marine Science. But it does minimize the light reaching those corals. The shade cloths reduced light by 60%. “While heat is the primary driver of coral bleaching, it also works synergistically with the light,” she says. “By minimizing that light, we’re cutting some of that stress that those corals are going through, and therefore minimizing bleaching.” [Photo: Courtesy NSU Florida] The impact of heat on coral reefs Climate change, and the warm ocean temperatures that come with it, are one of the biggest threats to coral reefs worldwide. More than 84% of the world’s reefs have been affected by heat stress, and half of all reefs have experienced major bleaching. The Florida Keys are no exception. In 2023, a marine heat wave had water temperatures hitting over 90 degrees Fahrenheit. (That coincided with an El Niño year; 2026 is also an El Niño year, which is supercharging oceans already warmed by climate change.) That summer, Florida’s coral reef experienced “the worst coral bleaching event ever recorded,” according to the state’s Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission . Neely has long monitored Florida’s coral reefs for heat stress and damage, but that 2023 bleaching event prompted the idea, she says, “that maybe we need to be a little more proactive in how we can deal with some of these stressors.” Shading coral reefs isn’t a totally new concept; researchers have looked into this technique in Australia, for the Great Barrier Reef, as well as in various places in the Indo-Pacific region. But there are different species of corals around the world, and it hadn’t been tried before in the Caribbean or around Florida. [Photo: Karen Neely] Underwater umbrellas Neely and her team ran the shading experiment in the summer of 2024. They built frames out of PVC pipe, using shade cloths for the umbrellas. They attached the shades to rope, and tied them to eye screws that they put in the substrate around the corals. The shade umbrellas floated about 30 centimeters (12 inches) above the coral. Corals do need some light; the algae that live symbiotically with corals (and that give reefs their color) need to photosynthesize. When these algae die, that’s when a coral reef turns white, or bleached. But by minimizing the harsh Florida sun, particularly during the long, especially bright days of summer, “we’re really giving [coral reefs] a helping hand,” Neely says. The shaded corals essentially experienced as much light as they would usually get in the winter. “We’re just minimizing their stress,” she says. Neely wasn’t totally surprised that the shades helped protect the corals from bleaching, compared with the unshaded coral. What was surprising, though, was “how easy it was to be effective,” she says. “We honestly thought these shades were going to be a way bigger hassle, but they were surprisingly easy to install,” she says. “They came out really easy at the end of the study. They didn’t require a lot of maintenance. They didn’t really present any of the problems that we thought they might.” The researchers also didn’t observe any negative impacts from these shades to the larger ecosystem. [Photo: Courtesy NSU Florida] Keeping coral reefs alive Shading coral reefs with underwater umbrellas may be a simple way to mitigate coral bleaching, but it also may be tricky to scale up. Neely admits it’s a targeted approach, focused on protecting individual corals, even though there are millions of corals around the world. Still, it’s an example of a climate change intervention that can make a tangible impact now. Cutting fossil fuel use, on the other hand, takes time—and even if we were to end all fossil fuel use today, our climate would still be affected for years to come. Coral reefs take up less than 1% of the ocean floor but support 25% of the ocean’s biodiversity, and also provide food, tourism, and shoreline protection. For them, the immediate impact of an intervention of this kind is crucial. “Reefs are already not what they were 50 years ago, and there’s no indication that they’re going to go back to that,” Neely says. Intervention or mitigation efforts like this are also more cost effective than coral restoration. The researchers found that shading a coral costs about $100. If that coral died, though, replacing or restoring it would cost more than $1,000. “We can’t restore our way out of everything,” Neely says. “We have to try to keep what’s already out there alive, from a cost and effort perspective. Not to mention the fact that these are some of the largest, oldest animals on the planet.”

articles.title: 20% of Swiss Glaciers Lost In Five Years
articles.description: Swiss glaciers lost 5.5% of their ice volume in the first eight months of 2026, bringing total losses since 2021 to 19.4%. Researchers say some glaciers are now collapsing from within as meltwater carves out large cavities. The Guardian reports: Matthias Huss, a glaciologist at ETH Zurich and lead author of the report, said many people do not realize how fast glaciers are retreating, or that just one generation ago some now-barren sites used to sit beneath hundreds of meters of ice. The scientists have not yet compiled a formal tally of lost glaciers this year but said they had witnessed the death of a number of small ones. "I visited one last week and it's so impressive to stand in this moonlike landscape where there was a big layer of ice -- an extensive glacier -- just a few years ago," said Huss. "And now it's a rock desert where there's some scattered blocks of old ice still lying around and melting on the hot rocks." The report, a collaboration between the Swiss Glacier Monitoring Network and the Swiss Commission for Cryosphere Observation, found the mean thickness of individual glaciers fell by between 2.5 metres and 4 metres in 2026. Huss said scientists were increasingly seeing glaciers collapse from the inside -- the result of internal streams beneath the ice that excavate caverns -- rather than simply retreating from surface heat. [...] Analysis published by MeteoSwiss on Tuesday found the summer half-year from April to September was the hottest and driest it had been since records began in 1864. In that time, humanity has filled the atmosphere with 1.8tn tons of carbon dioxide and heated the planet by about 1.4C. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
